title: Prove R(3,l+1)/R(3,l) → 1 using recurrence + lower bound

problemStatement.plain: Prove that the ratio of consecutive Ramsey numbers R(3,l+1)/R(3,l) converges to 1 as l → ∞. Uses the Ramsey recurrence R(3,l+1) ≤ R(3,l) + (l+1) combined with the Kim-Shearer lower bound R(3,l) ≥ c·l²/log l.
whyMatters: Resolves the k=3 case of Erdős Problem #1014
Shows Θ bounds suffice when combined with recurrence (contrary to common belief)
Provides explicit convergence rate O(log l/l)

knownResults.goal: Eliminate the 1 remaining sorry on eventually_ratio_small (log l/l → 0)

currentState.focus: Proof essentially complete. 1 sorry on routine analysis lemma.
currentState.nextAction: Prove eventually_ratio_small using isLittleO_log_rpow_atTop from Mathlib.

knowledge.progressSummary: PROGRESS: Main theorem proved modulo 1 routine sorry. Key insight: recurrence bounds increment linearly while values grow quadratically/log.
builtItems: ratio_abs_eq in Erdos1014OQ01.lean: absolute value identity
insights: The Ramsey recurrence provides a tight O(l) bound on the increment R(3,l+1) - R(3,l)
Only the LOWER bound R(3,l) ≥ c·l²/log l is needed, not the upper bound
The Θ bounds DO suffice for k=3 when combined with the recurrence - the recurrence constrains increments independently of the Θ bounds
Rate of convergence is O(log l/l), which is tight up to constants
